## Learning goals

::: {.nonincremental}
- **Choose** a review type that fits your purpose
- **Explain** what a review can and cannot establish
- **Translate** a topic into a concept table and a Web of Science search string
- **Assess** a search: precision, recall, validation
- **Select** studies with explicit criteria; document it in a **PRISMA** flow diagram
- **Synthesise** with a concept matrix instead of summarising
- **Identify** biases in the literature, your search and your synthesis
- **Use** AI at each stage without giving up reproducibility
:::

## How this lecture works

::: {.dek}
Nine short chapters. Each ends with a question to check yourself; the tutorial
on the lecture page turns every chapter into a step you do yourself.
:::

- **Reference model:** the *systematic* literature review

- **Payoff:** the literature review section of *your* term paper or thesis

- **Pause tasks:** when you see one, stop the video and do it

- **Take-home II** follows the same steps — watch everything first

::: {.keybox .fragment}
You will rarely publish a systematic review. You will always write a review section.
:::

## One literature runs through the whole lecture

::: {.dek}
Capabilities and routines: a set of ideas that sits exactly at the intersection
of evolutionary economics and business studies — and that different
communities describe with different words.
:::

- **Routines** as the "genes" of the firm [@nelson1982evolutionary]

- **Absorptive capacity**: recognise, assimilate and apply external knowledge [@cohen1990absorptive]

- **Dynamic capabilities**: integrate, build and reconfigure competences
  in changing environments [@teece1997dynamic]

- **Routine dynamics**: routines as a source of change, not only of stability [@feldman2003reconceptualizing]

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Running question: *How do empirical studies conceptualise and measure
capabilities and routines when they explain firm-level innovation?*
:::

## What a review is for {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
01
:::

## A review is a study whose data are other studies

::: {.dek}
That is what separates a review from "reading around a topic": it has a
question, a method, and a result that someone else could check.
:::

- **Map** a field: who works on what, with which concepts and methods

- **Establish** what is known — and how robustly

- **Find** gaps, contradictions and under-studied contexts

- **Build** or refine a conceptual framework

- **Justify** your own research question

::: {.keybox .fragment}
A review answers a question. If you cannot state the question, you are not
reviewing yet.
:::

## Review as a method and review as a section are not the same thing

::: {.dek}
Same logic, different scale. The standards of the first make the second
better.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Review as a stand-alone study
:::

- The review **is** the contribution

- Full protocol, several databases, two screeners

- Reported with **PRISMA** in full

- Example: @schilke2018quo on dynamic capabilities
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Review as a section of your paper
:::

- The review **motivates** your contribution

- One database, a documented string, explicit criteria

- Reported in a **paragraph** plus flow diagram

- Your term paper, your thesis
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Borrow the discipline of the left column; scale it to the right one.
:::

## Choose the review type by purpose, not by prestige

::: {.dek}
Simplified from @snyder2019literature and @grant2009typology. Real reviews
mix types; the label matters less than being explicit about what you did.
:::

| Type | Purpose | Search | Synthesis | Example |
|:-----|:--------|:-------|:----------|:--------|
| Narrative | Overview, interpretation | Selective, often undocumented | Narrative | Textbook chapters |
| Integrative | New framework from diverse work | Purposive, documented | Conceptual | @becker2004organizational |
| Scoping | How big and varied is a field? | Broad, documented | Mapping, counts | @arksey2005scoping (method) |
| Systematic | Answer a focused question | Exhaustive, reproducible | Structured, often thematic | @lane2006reification |
| Meta-analysis | Pool effect sizes | Exhaustive | Statistical | @orlitzky2003corporate |
| Bibliometric | Structure of a field | Database export | Citation networks | — |

: {.tasks}

::: {.source}
Lane et al. analyse 289 papers from 14 journals; Becker reviews the routines
literature since Nelson and Winter; Orlitzky et al. pool studies on corporate
social and financial performance.
:::

## The capabilities literature has been reviewed in all of these ways

::: {.dek}
Which is useful: you can see what each type of review is able to deliver on
the same subject matter.
:::

- **Integrative**: @becker2004organizational — the routines literature is
  "riddled with ambiguities" about what routines are

- **Critical systematic**: @lane2006reification — absorptive capacity has
  been *reified*: widely used, rarely examined

- **Content-analytic**: @schilke2018quo — a meta-framework of antecedents,
  mechanisms and outcomes of dynamic capabilities

- **Meta-analysis**: not meaningful here — the concepts are measured too
  differently to pool

::: {.keybox .fragment}
The state of the literature constrains which review type is possible.
:::

## What a review can do

::: {.dek}
Five things a well-done review can legitimately claim.
:::

- **Map** a debate and the positions in it

- **Establish** how much evidence exists, and of which kind

- **Show** where results agree, conflict, or depend on context

- **Locate** gaps — relative to a documented search

- **Clarify** concepts that a literature uses inconsistently

## What a review cannot do

::: {.dek}
These limits hold however carefully you work. Saying so is a sign of
competence, not of weakness.
:::

- Produce **better evidence** than the studies it rests on

- **Prove** that something has not been studied — only that your search did
  not find it

- Be **objective** by being systematic: question, database, terms and
  criteria are choices

- **Settle** a causal question the primary studies could not settle

- Turn **frequency** of a claim into **evidence** for it

- Replace **reading** the key works

## Spotlight: a review can map the QWERTY debate, not settle it

::: {.dek}
Path dependence is a core idea of evolutionary economics. Its most famous
example has been contested for decades.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Lock-in
:::

- QWERTY persisted through technical interrelatedness, economies of scale
  and quasi-irreversibility [@david1985clio]

- Read as evidence that markets can lock in **inferior** standards
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
"Fable of the keys"
:::

- The evidence for Dvorak's superiority is weak and partly from Dvorak
  himself [@liebowitz1990fable]

- Read as evidence that the lock-in story is **not established**
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
A review can show which evidence each side rests on. Whether Dvorak is faster
is a question for primary research.
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 1 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox}
A fellow student writes: "My systematic review shows there is no research on
dynamic capabilities in family firms." Which two things from this chapter
should make you sceptical — and how should the sentence be rewritten?
:::

## Workflow and question {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
02
:::

## A systematic review has six stages — and the first is decided before you search

::: {.dek}
The order matters because each stage constrains the next. Changing the
question after seeing the results is the review equivalent of p-hacking.
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[1 Protocol · 2 Search]{.caphead}

Question, scope and criteria **written down first**; then the documented search.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[3 Screening · 4 Extraction]{.caphead}

Apply criteria to titles, abstracts and full texts; record what each study
says in a fixed format.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[5 Synthesis]{.caphead}

Organise findings by concept, not by author; explain agreement and
disagreement.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[6 Reporting]{.caphead}

What you did, what you found, and what your choices may have cost you.
:::
:::

::: {.source}
Following @tranfield2003towards, who adapt the medical template to
management research.
:::

## A topic is not a question

::: {.dek}
"Capabilities and innovation" is a topic. A reviewable question names what you
look at, in which context, and what you want to know about it.
:::

- **Too broad:** "What do we know about capabilities?"

- **Too narrow:** "Does absorptive capacity raise patenting in German
  biotech SMEs in 2015?"

- **Reviewable:** "How do empirical studies conceptualise and measure
  capabilities and routines when they explain firm-level innovation?"

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Test: could two people, given your question, agree on whether a paper is in or out?
:::

## The concept table turns the question into building blocks

::: {.dek}
One column per concept in the question, one row per way of saying it. This
table becomes your search string in the next chapter.
:::

| Capabilities & routines | Innovation | Empirical measurement |
|:------------------------|:-----------|:----------------------|
| dynamic capabilit\* | innovat\* | measur\* |
| organi?ational routine\* | "new product\*" | operationali?ation |
| absorptive capacit\* | patent\* | empiric\* |
| organi?ational capabilit\* | R&D | survey\* |
| technological capabilit\* | | "panel data" |
| competenc\* | | |

::: {.source}
`*` = any ending, `?` = exactly one character (organisation / organization).
The third column could also be handled by criteria instead of the string — a
decision you have to document.
:::

## Criteria are fixed before you see the results

::: {.dek}
Inclusion and exclusion criteria are part of the protocol. Write them so
that a second person would make the same decision.
:::

- **Content:** studies that measure a capability or routine construct and
  relate it to innovation

- **Design:** empirical — quantitative or qualitative; conceptual papers out

- **Type:** peer-reviewed articles and reviews; book chapters out (and say why)

- **Period and language:** e.g. 1990 onwards, English — **a limitation you will report**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Every criterion is a decision that someone could disagree with. That is fine
— as long as it is visible.
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 2 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox}
Write down a reviewable question for your own term-paper topic and build a
concept table with at least two concepts and four terms each. You will need it
in the tutorial.
:::

## Searching {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
03
:::

## Not every search system is fit for a systematic review

::: {.dek}
A system is suitable only if it searches reliably, lets you formulate a
precise query, and returns the same results tomorrow.
:::

- **Web of Science**: curated, Boolean, reproducible, exportable — *our*
  database

- **Google Scholar**: huge coverage, but no full Boolean control, ranked and
  non-reproducible results

- Of 28 systems tested, only **14** met all requirements for systematic
  reviews [@gusenbauer2020which]

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Use Google Scholar to find a paper you know exists. Do not use it as your
search.
:::

## Three families of search tools work in different ways

::: {.dek}
The same distinction as in lecture 2 — here applied to where each tool fits
in a review.
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[Keyword (Boolean) search]{.caphead}

Web of Science. Finds what matches your terms. Transparent and
reproducible — and blind to words you did not think of.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Semantic (AI) search]{.caphead}

"Finders". Matches meaning, not words. Good for discovering vocabulary;
opaque ranking, not reproducible.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Citation-based search]{.caphead}

"Connectors". Follows references from seed papers. Finds what keywords miss
— within the citing community.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[In a review]{.caphead}

Boolean search is the **backbone**. Semantic tools **feed** the concept table.
Citation search **supplements** at the end.
:::
:::

## From concept table to search string

::: {.dek}
OR within a concept, AND between concepts. Field tag `TS=` searches title,
abstract and keywords.
:::

```text
TS=("dynamic capabilit*" OR "organi?ational routine*"
    OR "absorptive capacit*" OR "organi?ational capabilit*"
    OR "technological capabilit*")
AND
TS=(innovat* OR "new product*" OR patent*)
AND
TS=(measur* OR operationali?ation OR empiric* OR survey*)
```

- **Quotation marks** keep phrases together

- **Truncation** and **wildcards** catch spelling and endings

- **Filters** (years, document type, language) are documented separately

::: {.source}
Interface details and the full syntax are in the tutorial. Check the Web of
Science help on lemmatisation before relying on exact word forms.
:::

## Every search trades recall against precision

::: {.dek}
You cannot maximise both. Systematic reviews deliberately favour recall and
pay for it with screening effort.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Recall (sensitivity)
:::

- Share of all **relevant** papers that your search finds

- Low recall → your review is **incomplete** without you knowing it
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Precision
:::

- Share of **found** papers that are relevant

- Low precision → you screen **thousands** of irrelevant titles
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Widening a string raises recall and lowers precision. Narrowing does the
opposite.
:::

## You cannot measure recall directly — so test against known papers

::: {.dek}
You never know all relevant papers. But you know some. If your string misses
them, it misses others too.
:::

- Before searching: list **5–10 key papers** you know must be found

- Run the string: how many does it retrieve?

- **Missed one?** Look at its title and keywords — which term was missing?

- Revise, rerun, **log every version**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Illustrative: string v1 finds 5 of 8 known papers → add "competenc\*" and
"routine\*" variants → v2 finds 8 of 8.
:::

## Spotlight: in the capabilities literature, words follow communities

::: {.dek}
Overlapping ideas carry different names in evolutionary economics, strategic
management, organisation studies and development economics.
:::

- Evolutionary economics: **routines**, organisational **capabilities**
  [@nelson1982evolutionary]

- Strategic management: **dynamic capabilities**, resources, core
  **competences** [@teece1997dynamic]

- Organisation studies: **routine dynamics** [@feldman2003reconceptualizing]

- Development and innovation studies: **technological capabilities**,
  **absorptive capacity** [@cohen1990absorptive]

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Search only "dynamic capabilit\*" and your review reports one community's
view as the state of the field.
:::

## Snowballing finds what your keywords missed

::: {.dek}
Start from a few highly relevant included papers and follow citations in both
directions [@wohlin2014guidelines].
:::

- **Backward:** the reference lists of your seed papers

- **Forward:** papers that cite your seed papers (Web of Science: *Citing
  articles*)

- Apply **the same criteria** as for the database results

- Report snowballed papers **separately** in the flow diagram

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Snowballing supplements a documented search. It never replaces one.
:::

## Pause the video {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox}
Take your concept table from chapter 2 and write a first Web of Science string
(OR within, AND between concepts). Then name three papers that your string
must find. Do not run it yet — the tutorial walks you through that.
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 3 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox}
Your string returns 4,800 records. Your test set of eight key papers is found
completely. What does this tell you about recall and precision, and what are
your options?
:::

## Screening and selection {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
04
:::

## Screening happens in two rounds

::: {.dek}
Cheap decisions first, expensive ones later. Each round applies the criteria
from the protocol — not new ones.
:::

- **Round 1 — titles and abstracts:** exclude what is clearly out; when in
  doubt, keep

- **Round 2 — full texts:** decide on the remaining papers; **record the
  reason** for each exclusion

- **Second screener:** ideally on all records; at least on a sample —
  compare and discuss disagreements

- **Criteria drift:** if you find yourself changing a criterion, restart
  the round and document it

::: {.arrow .fragment}
A spreadsheet with one row per record and a column for the reason is enough.
The tutorial provides a template.
:::

## The PRISMA flow diagram shows what happened to every record

::: {.dek}
Illustrative numbers. The diagram is mandatory in a systematic review and the
easiest way to make your term paper's review checkable.
:::

| Stage | What is counted | n |
|:------|:----------------|--:|
| Identification | Records from Web of Science | 612 |
| Screening | Excluded on title / abstract | 540 |
| | Full texts sought / not retrievable | 72 / 3 |
| Eligibility | Full texts assessed / excluded with reasons | 69 / 41 |
| | *Reasons: not empirical (15), no innovation outcome (18), other (8)* | |
| Other sources | Added through snowballing | 6 |
| Included | Studies in the synthesis | 34 |

::: {.source}
Template: @page2021prisma. The R package PRISMA2020 draws the diagram from a
spreadsheet [@haddaway2022prisma2020] — see the tutorial.
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 4 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox}
Why should you record a reason for each full-text exclusion, but not for each
title/abstract exclusion? What could a reader do with those reasons?
:::

## From summary to synthesis {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
05
:::

## Most weak reviews are a list of summaries

::: {.dek}
Same three sources, two ways to write about them. The difference is whether
the paragraph is organised by author or by idea.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Author-centric
:::

- "Nelson and Winter (1982) describe routines as the genes of the firm.
  Teece et al. (1997) define dynamic capabilities as … Feldman and Pentland
  (2003) argue that routines …"

- Reader's question: **so what?**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Concept-centric
:::

- "The literature disagrees on whether routines stabilise or change firms.
  Early evolutionary work stresses stability (Nelson & Winter 1982); later
  work locates change *inside* routines (Feldman & Pentland 2003). Dynamic
  capabilities bridge both by …"

- The disagreement **is** the finding
:::
:::

## The concept matrix forces you to synthesise

::: {.dek}
Rows are studies, columns are concepts. Simplified illustration for four
foundational works [@webster2002analyzing].
:::

| Study | Construct | Level | Main emphasis | Evidence |
|:------|:----------|:------|:--------------|:---------|
| @nelson1982evolutionary | Routines | Firm | Stability, heredity | Theory, simulation |
| @cohen1990absorptive | Absorptive capacity | Firm | Cumulative learning from prior knowledge | Theory, R&D-based empirics |
| @teece1997dynamic | Dynamic capabilities | Firm | Reconfiguration for change | Conceptual |
| @feldman2003reconceptualizing | Routine dynamics | Routine | Change from within routines | Conceptual, field-based |

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Read the matrix by column, not by row: that is your synthesis.
:::

## Data extraction is where the matrix gets filled

::: {.dek}
Decide the columns before reading the full texts, pilot them on three papers,
then keep them fixed.
:::

- **Bibliographic:** authors, year, outlet

- **Design:** sample, country, period, method

- **Constructs:** how is the capability **defined**? how is it **measured**?

- **Findings:** direction, size, conditions

- **Quality notes:** what makes you trust this study more or less?

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Extraction is also where AI tools are tempting — and where silent errors
spread across the whole sample (chapter 7).
:::

## Spotlight: conflicting results on firm growth become informative once sorted

::: {.dek}
Gibrat's law says growth rates are independent of firm size. Decades of tests
give no single answer — but the disagreement is structured.
:::

- Results depend on **which firms** are in the sample — all, survivors only, or
  those above a minimum size [@mansfield1962entry]

- … and on **sector, size class, country and period** [@santarelli2006gibrat]

- A vote count (say, "12 for, 15 against") says **nothing**

- A matrix by sample and method shows **when** the law holds

::: {.source}
For a book-length synthesis see @coad2009growth. The lab's firm growth data
let you try this yourself.
:::

## Spotlight: when the same concept is measured differently

::: {.dek}
Related variety — technologically related industries in a region — has
become a central idea in evolutionary economic geography.
:::

- Introduced with an **entropy-based** measure [@frenken2007related]

- A review of **21** studies: most find that related variety supports
  employment growth; some only in knowledge-intensive sectors
  [@content2016related]

- Different **measures** and **levels** of relatedness across studies

- Synthesis has to ask: *same concept, or same word?*

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Pooling numbers that measure different things produces a precise answer to
no question.
:::

## Quality appraisal: not all included studies deserve equal weight

::: {.dek}
Formal appraisal tools come from medicine and fit management research only
partly. A short, explicit set of questions works better than none.
:::

- Is the **construct** clearly defined and measured consistently with it?

- Is the **design** able to support the claim (cross-section vs. panel,
  case vs. sample)?

- Is the **sample** described — and who is missing from it?

- Are **limitations** acknowledged by the authors?

## Check yourself — chapter 5 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox}
Take the literature review section of a paper you recently read. Is it
author-centric or concept-centric? Sketch the concept matrix its authors
*should* have built.
:::

## Biases, limitations, caveats {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
06
:::

## Bias enters at every stage of a review

::: {.dek}
Some biases are in the literature before you start. Others you introduce
yourself. A review can reduce the second kind and must report the first.
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[The literature]{.caphead}

Publication bias, citation bias, survivorship in the underlying samples.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Database and search]{.caphead}

Coverage bias, terminology bias, ranking and tool effects.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Screening]{.caphead}

Confirmation bias, single-screener judgement, criteria drift.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Synthesis and reporting]{.caphead}

Vote counting, apples and oranges, overclaiming from absence.
:::
:::

## The literature is a filtered sample of the research that was done

::: {.dek}
Significant, novel and positive results are more likely to be published. A
review that only reads what is published inherits this filter.
:::

- Across 159 empirical economics literatures, nearly **80%** of reported
  effects appear exaggerated, typically by a **factor of two**
  [@ioannidis2017power]

- CSR and profitability: a meta-regression of 512 studies finds a **small**
  positive effect and **publication bias** towards significant results
  [@hirsch2023csr]

- Compare an early meta-analysis reporting a clearly positive link
  [@orlitzky2003corporate]

::: {.arrow .fragment}
A review that counts published results measures the publication process as
much as the phenomenon.
:::

## Citation bias: often cited is not the same as well supported

::: {.dek}
Highly cited works attract more citations, and are increasingly cited for
what they are believed to say.
:::

- Absorptive capacity: Lane et al. analysed 289 papers and found the
  construct **reified** — used as given, rarely examined
  [@lane2006reification]

- Citation-based tools **amplify** this: they find what the community
  already cites

- AI summaries **amplify** it again: they reproduce the dominant reading

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Read the original. Then check whether the citing paper uses it the way the
original meant.
:::

## Survivorship bias: the studies you review may themselves be biased

::: {.dek}
A review inherits the sample problems of its primary studies — and can make
them invisible by aggregating.
:::

- Firm growth studies restricted to **surviving** firms drop the small firms
  that exited — so small firms look faster-growing than they are; the issue
  goes back to @mansfield1962entry

- Similar logic: studies of "successful" capability building rarely observe
  firms that tried and failed

- Synthesis has to **code** the sample design — otherwise the bias is averaged
  in

## Your database decides what can be found

::: {.dek}
Web of Science is curated. Curation is a selection, and the selection is not
neutral.
:::

- Web of Science and Scopus over-represent the **natural sciences** and
  **English-language** journals, and under-represent the **social sciences**
  and **humanities** [@mongeon2016journal]

- **Books** and **grey literature** are largely missing — a problem for
  economics and management, where working papers and books matter

- Research from the **Global South** is under-represented

::: {.arrow .fragment}
You cannot fix coverage with one database. You can test it with known papers
and report it.
:::

## Terminology bias is the pluralism problem of literature search

::: {.dek}
Your search terms encode a perspective. A string built from one school's
vocabulary silently excludes the others.
:::

- "Dynamic capabilities" ≠ "routines" ≠ "technological capabilities" — but
  overlapping ideas

- Heterodox and mainstream work often **name** the same phenomenon
  differently

- The result looks **systematic** and is still **one-sided**

- **Countermeasures:** harvest terms across communities, test alternative
  strings, compare hit lists

## You introduce bias yourself when you screen and synthesise

::: {.dek}
The reviewer is part of the instrument. The protocol exists to constrain
the reviewer.
:::

- **Confirmation bias:** borderline papers that fit your expectation stay in

- **Criteria drift:** the criteria change as you read

- **Vote counting:** counting significant results instead of weighing evidence

- **Apples and oranges:** pooling studies with different constructs and designs

- **Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Fixed criteria, a second screener, a concept matrix, careful wording — each
is a countermeasure.
:::

## Reporting, reproducibility, AI {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
07
:::

## A review must be reproducible from what you report

::: {.dek}
PRISMA 2020 lists 27 reporting items; PRISMA-S adds 16 items for the search.
For a term paper, the core fits into one paragraph and an appendix.
:::

- **Database** and date of the search

- The **full string**, including all filters

- **Criteria**, and who screened

- **Numbers** at each stage → flow diagram

- How you **synthesised** — and the **limitations** of all the above

::: {.source}
@page2021prisma; @rethlefsen2021prismas. The search log in the tutorial
records all of this as you go.
:::

## Write the limitations as specific as your method

::: {.dek}
"This review may not be complete" says nothing. Name the bias, the direction,
and why you accepted it.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Generic
:::

- "As with all reviews, some relevant studies may have been missed."
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Specific
:::

- "Restricting the search to English-language journal articles in Web of
  Science excludes the book-based and working-paper tradition of evolutionary
  economics; the review therefore likely over-represents the strategic
  management strand."
:::
:::

## AI helps at some stages and is risky at others

::: {.dek}
Classes as in lecture 2. The rule: AI may suggest; the documented, reproducible
step is yours.
:::

| Stage | AI can help with | Typical failure | Rule |
|:------|:-----------------|:----------------|:-----|
| Question, concept table | Synonyms, neighbouring vocabularies | Converges on the dominant terms | Check terms against key papers |
| Search | Discovering papers you missed | Opaque, non-reproducible results | Never the primary search |
| Screening | First sort of titles | Plausible but wrong exclusions | You decide; log reasons |
| Extraction | Reading many PDFs | Silent errors across the sample | Verify a sample by hand |
| Synthesis, writing | Structuring, critique of drafts | Generic, mainstream synthesis | Your matrix, your argument |

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Disclose every use — with the template from lecture 2.
:::

## Wrap-up {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
08
:::

## What to take away

- A review is a **study** with a question, a method and a checkable result

- **Concept table → string → test against known papers → log every version**

- **Synthesise** by concept; the concept matrix makes you

- Bias enters at **every** stage — reduce what you can, report the rest

- AI may **suggest**; the documented step is **yours**

::: {.keybox .lg .fragment}
Systematic does not mean objective. It means that your choices are visible.
:::

## Can and cannot, once more

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A review can
:::

- Map a debate — QWERTY, routines, Gibrat

- Show where results depend on context

- Locate gaps relative to a documented search
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A review cannot
:::

- Be better than its primary studies

- Prove that something has not been studied

- Turn frequency into evidence
:::
:::
